newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: World Bank says Bangladesh economy faces risks.
newsitem.headline: World Bank says Bangladesh economy faces risks.

text.p: The World Bank has warned that Bangladesh, tasting a spell of political stability, faced multiple risks while implementing reforms and pressing for speedy economic progress.
The warning came in a report by the bank's President James Wolfensohn to the Bangladesh government ahead of a two-day meeting of donors in Dhaka, starting on February 25.
Finance Minister S.A.M.S. Kibria will brief representatives of donor countries and agencies about the state of economy, policy reforms and objectives during the meeting, government officials said.
Wolfensohn in his report, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters, identified three major risks facing Bangladesh's economy.

First, he warned that political unrest could return and stall reforms. "The previous government is far from reconciled to its election defeat and its party may resort to street politics to destabilize the new government," he said.

"The Awami League government may have to redeem political debts that it incurred during its long absence from power and its election campaign (for exmaple, to trade unions and private business interest), and this could slow down parts of the reform agenda, such as in privatization, banking and trade policy," he added.
He further warned that the current account deficit and international reserve will come under pressure if overall aid disbursements do not recover and export growth trails behind imports.

Officials said the February 25-26 briefing was important as it would take stock of the country's macro-economic progress, reforms in administrative, banking and financial sectors, and denationalisation.

"They will review the first eight months' progress of the new government of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina and will also try to learn about the future plans of the government," a senior World Bank official in Dhaka told Reuters this week.
"The donors viewed this midterm review (ahead of annual aid club meeting) as very significant," the official said.
Hasina took over the government on June 23 after her Awami League won the general election.
A Bangladeshi official said the donors might criticise the government "as it has failed to fulfil committments regarding disinvestment as well as administrative reform."
"Although the government is sincere in its reforms commitment, it has yet to layout a definite work plan," he said.
The annual aid club meeting is held in Paris every April, but this year it will be held in Dhaka in September, World Bank and government officials said.

They said the change of venue and time was agreed at the request of Bangladeshi government because political opponents often crticise the party in power for "preparing annual budget only after the donors make commitments in the Paris consortium meeting."
